prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The corridor extends forward between close walls and glass storefronts, while a nearby person stays roughly 0.5–1.5 m from the camera, moving from the far left edge to center-left and then becoming partly cropped on the left again; a second person remains about 4–7 m ahead. The brighter foreground silhouettes and wall bands distinguish what is within arm’s reach—mainly the nearby person and portions of the doorway or wall—from the darker corridor and distant people, which is harder to judge from RGB alone. The nearby person is mostly side-on or facing away rather than looking toward the camera, and their body repeatedly occludes the corridor behind them as the camera’s relative position changes. Metric distances are only rough because the map is relative monocular depth, and several walls, glass surfaces, clothing regions, and silhouette boundaries have flattened or inconsistent brightness that can give unreliable separations.
descriptions.segmentation: The map consistently isolates one or more people: a person partly outside the left edge in frame 1, a large nearby person around center-left in frames 2–4, and that person again cropped at the left in frame 5, with smaller people several metres farther down the corridor. It makes overlap explicit where the nearby person blocks distant floor, walls, and people, and it shows that the nearest person is within roughly 1 m while the smaller figures are approximately 4–7 m away, although segmentation itself does not directly measure distance. The labelled silhouettes help distinguish adjacent people and reveal partial bodies at image boundaries; frame 1 also marks a small region near the foreground person as a handbag. Large green regions labelled “train” across frames 2 and 4 are clearly unreliable for this indoor scene, and missed masks, holes, and incomplete outlines—especially around distant people and objects behind glass—limit spatial interpretation.
descriptions.pose: The skeleton map provides sparse body geometry: a partly cropped person at the far left in frame 1, a larger nearby upright figure around center-left in frame 2, and small or fragmentary detections toward the right in frames 4–5. Joint placement helps show limb direction, vertical body extent, and whether a detected body is side-on or turned away, while also making cropped limbs and body parts hidden by occlusion more apparent than in RGB; no clear pose shows a face directed toward the camera. The larger skeleton is consistent with a person within about 1–2 m, whereas the much smaller detections correspond to people several metres away, but the map cannot reliably establish metric distance or relationships to walls and objects because it omits the scene layout. It is highly unreliable across the sequence: most visible people receive no complete skeleton, frame 3 has none, frame 5 contains only a short fragment, and several joints or extremities are displaced or missing, so reach and turning can only be inferred for the most complete detections.
